title: NN/g, “Brutalism and Antidesign”
lede: A usability firm separates raw, stripped-down web brutalism from deliberately chaotic antidesign.
summary: Kate Moran’s 2017 NN/g article: brutalism echoes bare 1990s HTML; antidesign is a separate, chaotic branch.

evidence.note: Article text read on 2026-10-02. The byline and the date (5 November 2017, modified 30 April 2020) are in the page’s structured data. The example screenshots in the article were not inspected.

styles.note: The main design-authority source for the name, and the source of the split between the raw core and antidesign.

context: Definition: “Brutalism in digital design is a style that intentionally attempts to look raw, haphazard, or unadorned. It echoes early 1990s-style websites (think Craigslist and the Drudge Report).”
On form: “Sometimes this aspect of brutalism is expressed as bare-bones, almost naked HTML site with blue links and monochromatic Monospace text.”

It notes that Craigslist was plain from the late 1990s because of HTML and CSS limits, not by artistic choice, and that NN/g’s own site in 2000 used “an unadorned, protobrutalist style”. Justin Jackson’s blog is cited for “black and blue Monospace typography”.
Antidesign, “often also referred to as brutalism”, is described separately: no visual hierarchy, harsh colors, disorienting patterns, odd cursors, and distracting animation.
interpretation: This article sets the scope of [Brutalist web design](style:brutalist-web-design): the raw, readable core. The chaotic branch is antidesign and is not part of the style.
borrow: Use the article’s test: does the page feel raw because it shows its HTML, or because it is hard to use? Only the first is this style.
